newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: All eyes on S.Korean president after son's arrest.
newsitem.headline: All eyes on S.Korean president after son's arrest.

text.p: As his son spent his first day in prison on Sunday on bribery charges, South Korean president Kim Young-sam faced an uphill battle to redeem his own public image shattered by the scandal.

The arrest on Saturday of Kim Hyun-chul, the president's second son, on charges of taking bribes worth millions of dollars marked the beginning of the end of a prosecution inquiry into pervasive graft laid bare by the multi-billion dollar collapse of a leading steelmaker.
Further arrests were expected on Sunday, including a former security chief close to Kim Hyun-chul.

Meanwhile, news reports said prosecutors would on Monday demand sentences for 11 people on trial for bribery in connection with the failure of Hanbo Steel Co in January, among them three close aides of the president.
But while legal proceedings in what has become known as "Hanbogate" wind down, the woes of a president who took power vowing to erase graft are far from over.
There are lingering suspicions that the prosecution deliberately stopped short of probing political links between Hanbo and President Kim Young-sam.
Opposition politicians allege that the Hanbo affair is at root a political scandal connected to the funding of president Kim's 1992 election campaign, which his son helped manage.

They allege the campaign was partly financed by a 90 billion won ($101 million) gift from the chairman of the Hanbo Group, Chung Tae-soo, and that loans of five trillion won to his steelmaking flagship were to repay the favour.
State prosecutors were unable to establish any direct involvement by Kim Hyun-chul in the loans-for-kickbacks scandal swirling around Hanbo Steel.

Instead, they charged him with accepting 3.2 billion won of bribes from unrelated businesses, and with failing to pay tax on 3.3 billion won he took as gifts. He faces a maximum sentence of life in jail for tax evasion, and five years for bribery, and is now being held in the Seoul Detention House.
"Hyun-chul's arrest is not the end," the Dong-A Ilbo newspaper said in an editorial.
"Suspicions regarding his alleged involvement in the Hanbo loan scandal and his management of leftover funds from the 1992 presidential election are still left under a fog."
The opposition claims that the former security chief, Kim Ki-sup, managed as much as 10 billion won in unspent campaign donations on behalf of the younger Kim.
"President Kim Young-sam has to make an understandable apology and confession to the public regarding his son and the election fund," the Joongang Ilbo daily said.
Media reports on Sunday speculated that the president would make a statement on election donations during a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, and apologise again over his son.
But few South Korean believe a detailed accounting will be forthcoming, or is even possible.
Some political analysts have suggested the president will confine himself to remarks regretting old-style money politics and promising campaign financing reform.

The president on Saturday wasted no time in trying to portray his son's arrest as evidence of his commitment to clean government, despite the evidence of corruption and influence-peddling all around him.
"President Kim again expressed regrets that the public has been given such a severe shock and disappointment through this incident," a presidential Blue House statement said.
"This reflects President Kim's firm intention that there should be no sanctuary when it comes to punishing corruption," it added.
"From now on, President Kim will sternly punish, according to the law and regardless of status or social rank, those linked to corruption." ($1 = 891 won)
